analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers from charging women higher premiums than men for the same coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill to bar insurers from pricing premiums by gender sat in two House committees without a hearing or vote, and a nearly identical ban became law a year later through the Affordable Care Act.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal health insurance rules so a health plan could not charge a woman a higher premium or contribution than a similarly situated man, in both employer plans and individually purchased insurance. Insurers in the individual market commonly used 'gender rating,' charging women more in part because their expected care costs were higher. The bill would also order the Government Accountability Office to study how well the existing federal protections in these markets are actually enforced.
analysis.who_benefits: Women, especially those who buy health insurance on their own rather than through an employer, who under then-common pricing practices could be charged noticeably higher premiums than men of the same age and health status for identical coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women buying their own health insurance

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans from charging any individual a premium or contribution greater than a similarly situated enrollee's on the basis of gender, effective for plan years starting 6 months after enactment.
Extends the same gender-rating prohibition to individually purchased health insurance, where gender rating was most widely used.
Directs the Comptroller General to study and report on how effectively the existing federal health insurance market rules are enforced, with recommendations for improvement.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers give up the ability to set premiums by gender, and the cross-subsidy within plans shifts: premiums for some men, particularly younger men, would rise as women's premiums fall, with total plan revenue roughly unchanged.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers' rating flexibility; some male enrollees

drawbacks.text: Banning gender rating is a cross-subsidy: because women's expected care costs are on average higher, premiums that no longer vary by gender rise for some men, especially younger men, while falling for women.
Insurers argued that actuarial pricing by expected cost is what keeps premiums aligned to risk, and a blanket prohibition removes one rating factor without addressing underlying cost drivers.
The bill provided no mechanism to offset the shift in premiums between groups, relying on the overall pooling of risk to absorb it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For women facing surcharges, the benefit is direct and immediate: identical coverage at the same price as a man. The cost is real but narrower — some men's premiums rise as part of the same pooling — and the bill is a modest, narrowly drawn fix rather than a restructuring of the market. Its main weakness is that Congress enacted essentially the same prohibition through the ACA in 2010, so the policy idea had broader support than this particular bill's fate suggests.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced and then to an Energy and Commerce health subcommittee, and neither committee took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the Gender Equity in Health Premiums Act on May 21, 2009, with five original cosponsors including Republican Rep. Ginny Brown-Waite.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, splitting jurisdiction between them.
On June 2, 2009, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 111th Congress.
The bill attracted 14 cosponsors — 12 Democrats and 2 Republicans — but never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.
Congress enacted a comparable prohibition on gender rating for the individual market as part of the Affordable Care Act in 2010, addressing the same problem this bill targeted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept gender rating for the remainder of the Congress, though the practice was largely eliminated a year later when the ACA took up the same idea. Committee leaders avoided having to act on the standalone bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers kept gender rating until the ACA stepped in

for.name: Rep. Linda Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a small bipartisan group of cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Ginny Brown-Waite
for.what_they_did: One of two Republican cosponsors, signing on the day of introduction.

for.name: 12 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat beyond this group moved it forward.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and referred it to its Health Subcommittee, then took no further action for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for its jurisdiction over the tax-code provisions and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote to measure party splits; sponsorship was bipartisan but thin, with 12 of 253 House Democrats and 2 of 178 House Republicans cosponsoring.

industries.note: The bill removes gender from the list of factors insurers may use to set premiums, ending the practice of charging women more for identical coverage. Insurers lose pricing flexibility, and the change shifts premium burden toward some male enrollees rather than reducing insurer revenue overall.
